title: Buried Talents
author: Edan Krolewicz
summary: Edan Krolewicz, an MIT-trained insider, argues that America's elites, defined by cognitive ability, wealth, institutional standing and social capital, have used very little of that advantage on hard public problems. He is careful to say that elites are not villains and that he is not against conventional lifestyles; his complaint is about what goes unused. He walks through types of elite: the credentialed professionals who say they will do something meaningful later, the capital holders whose money compounds in index funds, the retired who have all the time in the world, the idea makers whose incentives reward citations and engagement over relevance, and the opt-outs. For each he shows how a standing excuse such as the mortgage, "being strategic" or "later" collapses on inspection, and he notes that retirees with professional skills could fill gaps in local government, nonprofits and school boards. He admits he is in the middle of uncertain work himself and asks the reader what they would do if they took the question seriously, whether ten hours a week or a changed career.
points: Elites are defined by four assets, ability, money, institutional standing and networks, which few people hold in full but many hold in part.
The problem is not harm but inaction: skills and freedom are stored energy pointed at personal advancement and comfort.
Each excuse, "once the mortgage is gone", "I want to be strategic", "I will do it later", is a moving threshold that justifies staying put.
Retired professionals are the cleanest test case, since the usual constraints are gone, and civic institutions badly need their skills.
The aim is practical: a peer group, a specific task, a gradient instead of a cliff, and proof the leap is survivable.
quotes: I’m thirty-five years old. I graduated from MIT with degrees in computer science and management. Bootstrapped a company as a solo founder and made enough to not worry about money for a while.
Most are decent by conventional measures. To be clear, the problem isn’t that they’re causing harm. The problem is that they’re not doing anything with what they’ve been given.
Governance doesn’t work this way. Public health doesn’t work this way. Democracy is not a pure engineering problem.
The 4 hour work week lifestyle designers built lives around personal freedom. No bosses, no commutes, days structured around exercise and projects and travel.

Harm avoidance. Private virtue. It draws on liberalism’s deepest ideas: the individual as the center of meaning, the family as the core obligation, the public sphere as a space of tolerance rather than shared purpose.
The swimmer isn’t morally superior. They’re differently positioned. Ability is relevant to what you should do.
The other half I feel lost. Unsure whether any of it matters. Wondering if I should go back to scaling SaaS companies where the metrics were at least clear.

Your institutional knowledge—how to manage a budget, run a meeting, navigate a bureaucracy—is worth more than most nonprofits’ annual consulting spend. Twenty hours a week would transform an organization.
